Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

randomPlantedForest (development version)

Breaking changes

  • rpf() has new defaults: a plain rpf(y ~ ., data) now returns the pruned model (class rpf_pruned), for regression and classification. The new defaults, each switched by its argument:

    • n_splits = NULL: the number of splits is chosen out of bag while the forest grows (was 30).
    • prune = NULL: the forest is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults, and every kept component of three or more predictors is shown in at most max_panels = 10 heat maps (was no pruning). With deterministic = TRUE it means prune = FALSE and n_splits = NULL means 30, as there are no out-of-bag rows.
    • n_try_split_points = NULL, share_candidates = NULL: 3 thresholds per candidate and 10% of the possible splits per round for split_structure = "leaf" (was 10 / 0.4, still the default of the other split structures). This less greedy search is usually more accurate.
    • The split candidates of "leaf" are drawn by the fast draw (options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE), now the default): the same distribution as the exact draw, with other random numbers, so the same seed gives another forest. It is faster on larger data.
    • max_interaction = 3 (was 2). Order 3 is often more accurate than order 2; no limit (order p) is often much slower, and usually not more accurate.
    • n_families = 200 (was 50): more families usually lower the test error and give sparser pruned models. The loss is "L2" for regression and, as below, now "logit" for classification. So every default fit changes, regression and classification, and rpf() returns an rpf_pruned object instead of an rpf unless prune = FALSE. To fit a regression forest as before, give the previous defaults and the exact draw:
    options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = TRUE)
rpf(..., max_interaction = 2, n_families = 50, n_splits = 30, n_try_split_points = 10, share_candidates = 0.4, prune = FALSE)

    Classification fits of earlier versions cannot be reproduced this way: they change for every split structure and loss (see Bug fixes: classification uses regression’s split structures, the largest value of a predictor can be split off, and three or more classes with the exponential loss use SAMME). The default call does more work than before, so it takes more time and memory.

  • The classification losses "logit" and "exponential" (binary, and SAMME for three or more classes) no longer clamp class shares, and rpf()’s arguments delta and epsilon are removed: a call that gives either is an error (an unused argument). Each new leaf’s step now minimises the leaf’s penalised loss: the loss of its rows, plus that of one pseudo-row, split evenly over the classes, at the leaf’s current mean score (?rpf, “Classification losses”). A split is scored by its gain over the parent leaf’s own step, and each new leaf pays for its pseudo-row. So a leaf of one class converges to a finite level (log(2 n + 1) for n rows and two classes) and is not moved again, instead of being split and pushed further in every round; splitting such a leaf, or repeating a split whose leaves are at their optimum, gains nothing and is not made; and a round in which no candidate gains makes no split. Previously the split criterion credited a split with the parent leaf’s own step at a class share clamped to [delta, 1 - delta], while the update clamped it to [epsilon, 1 - epsilon], so pure and nearly pure leaves won over splits that separate classes, and logit’s leaves reset the mean score to the log-odds of the raw share, which is not a step of the loss and left fits underconfident. With the defaults (n_splits out of bag, pruning) the test log-loss usually changes little. At fixed split counts the exponential loss no longer overfits as it did; on noisy data with many splits both losses can fit the noise more than the clamped logit loss did, which the out-of-bag choice of n_splits avoids. rpf() gains exact_step (default TRUE): logit’s two new leaves get the exact minimisers of their penalised loss (Newton’s method to convergence on the leaf’s rows); FALSE takes one Newton step. The exponential loss’s step is exact by itself, so exact_step does not change its fits. The split search scores a candidate from sums over its two sides built as regression builds them (along the leaf’s sorted rows, or per bin), so classification fits are faster. Classification fits with "logit" or "exponential" change; "L1" and "L2" fits and regression are unchanged, and a model saved before still loads, prints and predicts.

  • The default classification loss is now "logit" (loss = NULL), with two classes and with more; it was "exponential" (with more than two classes SAMME). So every default classification fit changes; loss = "exponential" gives the previous default, which stays available and unchanged. The test log-loss of "logit" is usually as low as that of "exponential" or lower, more so with three or more classes. With many classes "exponential" can need many more splits.

  • A pruned model no longer holds the forest it was pruned from: rpf() with pruning (the default) and prune_components() return the model without it, and their new argument keep_forest = TRUE keeps it. The model predicts, prints and gives its components from what it stores, bit for bit as with the forest, so predict() (every type), predict_components(), print(), the display, rpf_marshal() and bundle() work as before; the fit itself is unchanged. What is lost by default is the forest in $fit: pruning it again (prune_components(model$fit, data, ...)), purify(), and the forest’s own predict(), predict_components(), plot() and rpf_boxes() are an error that names keep_forest = TRUE. $fit still describes the forest ($params, $oob_path, $splits_oob, the blueprint), and prune_components()’ caller still has the forest it passed. To get the forest back, fit with keep_forest = TRUE, or with prune = FALSE and prune with prune_components(). With prune = FALSE the argument has no effect. The forest’s memory is free when rpf() returns, and the model is a fraction of the forest’s size; the model without its forest is plain R data, so saveRDS() and readRDS() give a model that predicts, and rpf_marshal() is quick and gives a blob of the model’s size. Models saved with their forest by an earlier version (rpf_marshal()) still load, print and predict, and keep their forest.

  • With three or more classes, loss = "logit" now reports one score per class, summing to 0 across the classes, as "exponential" does: predict(type = "link") (and "numeric") has a column .pred_<level> for every level, predict_components() a column <component>__class:<level> for every component and level, and one intercept and one remainder column per level (target_levels lists all levels), and rpf_boxes() a column value_<level> for every level; the same for pruned models, whose print() shows one intercept per level. Before, the first level was the reference class and had no column (K - 1 columns for K levels). The new scores are the old ones with the first level’s score 0 joined and centred across the K classes, so a class’s score is now its log-odds against the geometric mean of all classes’ probabilities, not against the first class. The fit, its probabilities and classes, the out-of-bag choices and the pruned model (which components are kept, and their coefficients) do not change, and a model saved before loads and predicts the same probabilities; only what is reported changes. plot(class = NULL) now draws the first level, which has values of its own. To get the old scores back, subtract the first level’s column from every column and drop it. Two classes are unchanged: one score, the log-odds of the second level.

  • A pruned model of three or more classes with loss = "exponential" and rule "R" now reports its intercepts centred across the classes, so that its scores sum to 0 as the forest’s do: predict(type = "link"), the intercept of predict_components() and print(). Rule "R" fits them with the first class’s at 0, so its scores did not sum to 0 (by up to 3.7 on a simulated three-class set); the probabilities, classes and the stored intercept do not change.

Renamed arguments

  • Four arguments of rpf() and the split structures have clearer names; the prefix gives the unit (n_ a count, share_ a share in (0, 1], max_ a cap):
    • ntrees → n_families (the number of tree families),
    • splits → n_splits (splits per tree family),
    • split_try → n_try_split_points (split points tried per candidate),
    • t_try → share_candidates (share of the possible splits drawn as candidates each round);
    • split_structure: "leaves" → "leaf", "hist" → "leaf_binned", "cur_trees_1" → "tree_then_leaf", "cur_trees_2" → "tree_then_all_leaves", "res_trees" → "target_tree_then_leaf" (the candidate, then how the leaf to split is found).
  • The old names still work and give the same fit, with a deprecation warning once per session for each old name (class lifecycle_warning_deprecated; options(lifecycle_verbosity = "warning") warns every time, "quiet" never); giving an argument under both names is an error. The same holds for oob_path_checkpoints(splits = ) and for a tune_control() ladder with the columns split_try and t_try.
  • The new names are used in print(), in the tables of the new features (the n_splits column of $oob_path, the tuning’s $tune$search and $tune$settings, greediness_ladder()), and in errors and documentation. A fitted model’s $params keeps the old names (ntrees, splits, split_try, t_try and the old split_structure values), so code that reads them, and models saved by 0.5.0, keep working.

New features

  • Classification forests with loss = "logit" or "exponential" get a level: after the fit, one constant per score column, the maximum-likelihood intercept of the log-loss given the forest’s out-of-bag scores, so that every class’s mean out-of-bag probability is its frequency in the training rows. It is stored in every tree family’s null leaf, so it is part of the intercept of the forest, of its purification and of its pruned model; $level holds it and print() shows it (?rpf, “The level of the classification losses”). The families are averaged on the score scale, and where they disagree the probability of their mean score is below the mean of their probabilities for a class rarer than 1/2, so the forest predicted a rare class too rarely, the more so the more splits it made. With the level the forest predicts each class about as often as it occurs, at any number of splits. The out-of-bag choice of n_splits scores every number of splits at its own level, and the pruning starts from the forest with its level. This changes every fit with these losses, binary and multiclass; options(randomPlantedForest.level = FALSE) fits without the level.

  • rpf() gains keep_level_order, to keep the level order of factor predictors instead of ordering their levels by the outcome. TRUE keeps it for every factor, ordered or not, and a character vector for the named factors only; splits then separate neighbouring levels in the order of levels(). The default, FALSE, orders every factor by the outcome as before, and fits are unchanged. The coding is stored in $factor_levels, which predict(), predict_components() and purify() use, and print() names the factors that keep their order. The details of ?rpf describe how factor predictors are coded.

  • plot() draws the trees of one tree family to illustrate how a Random Planted Forest predicts. type = "tree" draws a split diagram in the style of Figure 1b of the paper, reconstructed from the fitted leaves, type = "boxes" draws the leaves in variable space, before or after purification. rpf_boxes() returns the leaves as a data frame. Requires ggplot2, and patchwork for type = "boxes". The “Getting started” vignette uses it to show how a tree family is built and what purification does.

  • prune_components() prunes the purified components of a forest (regression or classification; see the classification entry below). A component is kept if its share of the variance of the prediction on the training rows is at least tau. Rule "D" drops the others; rule "R" also refits the intercept and one coefficient per kept component by least squares, which changes their scale but not their shape. The rule and tau are chosen out of bag by default (select_by = "oob"), without refitting: one purification evaluates every tree family’s components at the training rows outside its bootstrap sample, and each candidate is scored by its out-of-bag RMSE, corrected for the extra variance of averaging fewer families. The out-of-bag choice usually picks the cross-validated model, or one about as good, in a fraction of the time. select_by = "cv" chooses by K-fold cross-validation instead, refitting the forest on each fold; by default it is used below 10 tree families and for deterministic forests. By default the largest tau whose error is within one standard error of the lowest is chosen (select = "1se"; select = "min" takes the lowest). With select_by = "oob", the coefficients of rule "R" are fitted on the out-of-bag components, to score each candidate, for the final model and for a given rule and tau, because the forest’s own components have also fitted the training rows’ noise; with select_by = "cv" they are fitted in sample. This sparse default is usually more accurate than the lowest out-of-bag error with in-sample coefficients, with far fewer components; it can drop a small true component. By default every kept component of three or more predictors is then shown in at most max_panels = 10 heat maps, and the model is pruned again with the shown components (max_panels = Inf switches this off). Two predictors of such a component stay at full resolution; the others are cut into intervals of equal numbers of training rows whose counts multiply to at most max_panels (a count of 1 averages a predictor out), the component is averaged within the cells (weighted by the product of the coarse predictors’ training marginals; the result is used as it is, not purified again), and the cuts that keep most of its variance are taken. The same rule then prunes again, so that the pruning judges the model that is shown; predictions use the coarsened components, and tau is then a share of that model’s variance. This is usually a little more accurate than coarsening after pruning, or than not coarsening. Every fit records how often each training row is in each family’s bootstrap sample (fits are unchanged), and rpf_marshal(include_data = TRUE) stores these in-bag counts. The pruned model is often both sparser and more accurate than the unpruned forest. The result, of class rpf_pruned, has methods for predict(), predict_components() (now an S3 generic) and print(), and works with rpf_marshal(), rpf_unmarshal() and bundle().

  • rpf(oob_path = TRUE) gives the out-of-bag error along the splits from one fit, in $oob_path (for classification the loss’s criterion, see below). With the same seed, the forest with k splits is exactly the first k splits of a forest with more, so while each tree family grows, its prediction at the training rows outside its bootstrap sample is updated split by split. The table has the plain and the corrected out-of-bag RMSE (the correction of prune_components()) at four checkpoints per doubling of the splits (oob_path_checkpoints()), or at given ones. Choosing n_splits by the lowest corrected error among the values of a cross-validation grid usually does as well as 5-fold cross-validation over that grid. The fitted forest is the same as without oob_path, which is off by default.

  • rpf(n_splits = NULL) chooses the number of splits out of bag while the forest grows (regression and classification). The forest’s corrected out-of-bag error is followed at four checkpoints per doubling of the splits, growing stops once its lowest value is one doubling back (at most 25,600 splits), and the forest at the lowest error is returned: the forest that rpf() with that many n_splits and the same seed gives. This usually chooses the same n_splits as the lowest error along a long fixed budget of splits, while growing fewer. The tree families grow one at a time, nthreads together, and keep only their out-of-bag predictions and a 40-byte record per split, from which the chosen forest is rebuilt without a refit; options(randomPlantedForest.adaptive_pause_gb) (0.25 GB) bounds the memory of families waiting for the stop. print() shows the chosen n_splits and where growing stopped. It is the new default (see Breaking changes). A corrected out-of-bag error at or below 0 at a checkpoint (a correction that overshot; never observed) is not chosen unless all are. A family waiting for the stop pauses at most one doubling past the first families’ estimate and grows on if the stop comes later, so a flat out-of-bag curve no longer makes every family grow far past the stop, with the same forest. Growing also stops once the error is on a plateau: once its lowest value has improved over the last doubling by at most one standard error of that improvement (paired over the training rows; options(randomPlantedForest.adaptive_tolerance), 1 by default, 0 for the stop on a new minimum alone). The choice is still the lowest error among the splits grown, so the plateau stop changes the forest only where the lowest error would have come later. It usually chooses the same n_splits as the stop on a new minimum alone, and grows fewer splits. The families grow only to about the plateau stop, so the fit often takes less time; where the families waiting for the stop do not fit in the pause budget, they grow on to the estimate of the stop on a new minimum, as a regrowth from their seed would cost more.

  • rpf(prune = TRUE) returns the pruned model instead of the forest (regression and classification): the forest is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults on the training rows, including the display at max_panels (a new argument of rpf(), 10 by default, Inf for no coarsening). The result equals prune_components(rpf(..., prune = FALSE), data) bit for bit from the same random number state, for the formula, x/y and recipe interfaces. With n_splits = NULL, one call chooses the number of splits out of bag, prunes and returns the model to show. prune = TRUE is an error with deterministic = TRUE, and purify is not used with it. It is the new default (prune = NULL, see Breaking changes); prune = FALSE returns the forest as before.

  • rpf() gains min_leaf_rows, the minimum number of rows on each side of every split, so in every leaf. Every split structure takes it, in regression and classification; the default 1 imposes no limit. Split points are tried only among those that keep this many rows on each side, and leaves without one are no longer drawn: as split candidates with "leaf" and "leaf_binned", by the leaf draw of "tree_then_leaf" and "target_tree_then_leaf" (a leaf’s weight is its number of such split points), and "tree_then_all_leaves" skips them. Binary predictors are split whenever both sides keep enough rows. The default min_leaf_rows = 1 fits the same models as before, bit for bit.

  • Classification with split_structure = "leaf" (the default) takes the fast draw of split candidates (options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE)) as regression does, and min_leaf_rows with every split structure. Both use regression’s draw: the same candidates are left out, and a classification fit with loss = "L2" on a 0/1 response is the regression fit, bit for bit, with either option. With min_leaf_rows = 1 and the exact draw (the default before this version) classification fits are unchanged, bit for bit.

  • rpf(tune = TRUE) tunes out of bag in one call (regression and classification): the greediness of the split search (n_try_split_points and share_candidates, on the ladder of the new greediness_ladder()) and min_leaf_rows. Every forest of the search has n_splits chosen out of bag and is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults, and the forest whose pruned model has the lowest corrected out-of-bag error wins; the display (max_panels) is applied once, to the chosen model. The search is coordinate-wise, about 10 forests: the ladder from 10 / 0.4 to 1 / 0.0125, then min_leaf_rows 1, 5, 20 and 100, then the two ladder neighbours of the chosen point. tune = "quick" grows two forests, 3 / 0.1 and 1 / 0.025, and the new tune_control() sets your own search. The result is the chosen forest’s pruned model, with the search table in $tune. The full search often lowers the test error clearly against 10 / 0.4, and does as well as 5-fold cross-validation over the same settings, or better, at a small fraction of its cost; the quick preset gets most of the gain. The default stays tune = FALSE.

  • Classification forests go through the same pipeline as regression forests: rpf(oob_path = ), rpf(n_splits = NULL), prune_components() with its display (max_panels), rpf(prune = TRUE) and rpf(tune = ). Every out-of-bag choice is scored by the loss’s own criterion, corrected for the out-of-bag family count: for loss = "L1" and "L2" the squared error of the raw scores summed over the classes (the Brier score), for "logit" and "exponential" the log-loss of the probabilities that predict(type = "prob") returns, with the correction in its second-order form. The corrected out-of-bag log-loss is usually close to the test log-loss, while the uncorrected one is above it. A component is kept or dropped for all classes, sized by its variance summed over the score columns centred across the classes; rule "R" fits one coefficient per kept component, shared by the classes, and one intercept per score column (least squares for the Brier score, maximum likelihood for the log-loss), out of bag; the display chooses one panel form per component for all classes. The pruned model’s predict() takes type as predict.rpf() does, and its predict_components() has one column per component and class. With two classes and loss = "L2", every choice is that of the regression pipeline on the 0/1 response, bit for bit. With the new defaults (see Breaking changes) a classification fit takes all these steps.

  • options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE) draws the split candidates of regression with split_structure = "leaf" from a tree of weights kept up to date between rounds, instead of one random number per possible split in every round (?rpf, “The draw of candidates for leaves”). This fits faster on larger data. It draws from the same distribution and leaves out the same candidates under min_leaf_rows, but with other random numbers, so the same seed gives another forest. TRUE (the default before this version) fits the same models as before, bit for bit.

  • rpf() gains interaction_constraints, a list of feature sets that restricts which interactions the forest may form, as in xgboost: a tree on the predictors T is grown only if T is a subset of one of the sets. The sets are given by predictor names or column indices (with a formula, indices follow the formula’s predictors; with a recipe, names only). They apply together with max_interaction, for every split_structure, in regression and classification, and print() shows them. The default NULL leaves fits unchanged.

  • print() of a pruned model shows the final model: its intercept and its components, largest first, each with its importance, its share of the variance of the model’s prediction on the training rows ($components$model_share, a new column: the coefficient times the component, in the form the model uses, over the model’s prediction; for classification over the centred score columns). share, what tau thresholds, is the forest’s component before the coefficient, so a component with a large coefficient is a larger part of the model than its share. How the components were chosen (the forest’s families and splits, given or chosen out of bag, the rule and threshold, what was left out, the heat-map forms) follows under “How it was chosen”. No choice or fit changes.

Bug fixes

  • prune_components() (and so rpf() with pruning) left the value of a tree family that made no split out of the pruned model’s intercept, so that rule "D" at tau = 0 was not the forest where a family had found no split. The intercept now includes it, as purify()’s does.

  • The out-of-bag path (oob_path, and the out-of-bag choice of n_splits) counted a tree family that had made no split at the score 0 its rows start from, instead of at the fit of its rows that the family predicts (the mean for regression and the L1 / L2 losses, the log-odds of its sample for "logit" and "exponential", so a probability of 1/2 instead). It now counts such a family at its fit. Families without a split are common only with a rare class and few rows, where they made the out-of-bag log-loss of few splits too high, so that the out-of-bag choice of n_splits could take far more splits than it should.

  • split_structure = "tree_then_leaf" samples leaves in proportion to their available thresholds, as documented. After a split, the sampling weights of new leaves counted rows instead of distinct values, and the cached prefix sums were built incorrectly. Leaves with tied values were then drawn too often, and draws were wasted on leaves that cannot be split. With deterministic = TRUE, "tree_then_leaf" evaluated only the first split candidate in every round; it now evaluates the first max_candidates, as the other split structures do. Fitted models change for regression with split_structure = "tree_then_leaf", random and deterministic.

  • split_structure = "target_tree_then_leaf" with deterministic = TRUE evaluates thresholds evenly spread over all (predictor, leaf, threshold) triples of a candidate. Previously it tried only the lowest thresholds of each leaf and left most of the variance unexplained. Fitted models change for regression with split_structure = "target_tree_then_leaf" and deterministic = TRUE only.

  • split_structure = "tree_then_all_leaves" with deterministic = TRUE evaluates n_try_split_points thresholds evenly spread over each leaf, as "tree_then_leaf" does. Previously it tried the 1st to 9th smallest values of each leaf. Fitted models change for regression with split_structure = "tree_then_all_leaves" and deterministic = TRUE only.

  • Classification’s split structures were never completed to match regression’s. They now use the same candidate pool, the same sampling of candidates, leaves and thresholds, and the same aging; only the loss differs. With loss = "L2" a classification fit on a 0/1 response now equals the regression fit (same seed). Previously "tree_then_leaf" was "tree_then_all_leaves"; "target_tree_then_leaf" used another candidate pool and ignored split_decay_rate; "leaf_binned" only ever split the root, so it fitted an additive model of stumps whatever max_interaction was; and "tree_then_all_leaves" never split the candidate tree’s own leaves. The fixes above for "tree_then_leaf" sampling and for deterministic = TRUE apply to classification too. Classification fits change for every split_structure and every loss.

  • The internal loss "exponential_2" no longer crashes.

  • Splits can separate the largest value of a predictor within a leaf. Previously every split structure except "leaf" for regression excluded that split, so binary predictors were never split on, and classification could not learn from them at all. Fitted models change for classification and for regression with split_structure other than "leaf".

  • A tree family that makes no split predicts the mean outcome of its bootstrap sample, and for classification its rows’ fit (with loss = "logit" or "exponential" the class shares smoothed by the losses’ pseudo-row, see Breaking changes). Previously it predicted 0, a probability of 0.5: constant predictors, a single row or min_leaf_rows above half the rows gave an all-zero model, and families that could not split pulled the forest towards 0. purify() puts that value into the intercept. Fitted models change only where a family made no split.

  • The same holds when n_splits = NULL (the default) chooses the number of splits out of bag: a family without a split up to the chosen number predicts its rows’ fit instead of 0, as a fit with that n_splits does. The pruned model already got the level from its intercept; the forest in it ($fit) did not. Without n_splits = NULL, and for families with a split, fits are unchanged. The pruned model also no longer fails for classification when no component has any variance (for example, constant predictors).

  • Errors while fitting or purifying with nthreads > 1 are reported as R errors. Previously an error in a worker thread terminated the R session.

  • predict(type = "link") works for classification forests with loss = "L1" or "L2". It returns the raw predictions, as type = "numeric" does (the link is the identity). Previously it stopped with an error about the size of pred.

  • rpf() stops with a clear error on inputs that gave wrong fits without a warning or failed later: an infinite outcome, t_try = 0, predictor names that are missing, duplicated or contain :, and interaction terms in the formula. rpf() finds interactions itself, so write y ~ x1 + x2 instead of y ~ x1 * x2; to fit a product as a predictor of its own, write I(x1 * x2) or add it to the data as a column. A character or logical outcome and a factor outcome with a single class get the package’s own message instead of one from hardhat or model.matrix(). Unused levels of a factor outcome are dropped with a warning; previously a binary outcome with an unused level was fitted, but predict() failed. predict() on zero rows returns zero rows instead of an error.

  • The C++ code compiles without warnings under -Wall -pedantic.

  • predict_components() returns one intercept per target level for multiclass classification, named by target_levels (#70). Previously only the first level’s intercept was returned, so components plus intercept did not sum to the prediction for other levels.

  • predict_components() accepts a matrix as new_data, like predict() does. It no longer turns the caller’s data.frame into a data.table by reference.

  • predict() after purify(maxp_interaction = k) with k below the fit’s max_interaction returns the forest’s prediction. Previously it returned the intercept plus the components up to order k, leaving out the higher orders. predict_components() now returns their sum as remainder, so that its result sums to the prediction, and rpf_marshal() keeps the purification’s cap.

  • loss = "exponential" is with more than two classes the multiclass exponential loss SAMME (Zhu, Zou, Rosset and Hastie, 2009): the split criterion, the leaf step and the weights all come from the one loss exp(-y.f / K). Each row has one weight, exp(-g) with g its class’s score, and a leaf moves the scores by log(V_k) - mean_j log(V_j), with V its class weight sums plus those of its pseudo-row (see the classification losses under Breaking changes); predict() takes the softmax of the scores as before. Previously each class had its own one-vs-rest weights, and its step was log(p_k / p_0) with p_0 = 1 - sum_k p_k mixing shares under the different weights; it is 0 at the start and was clamped to epsilon, so every class’s score rose by a common log(1 / epsilon) that the softmax ignores but the weights did not. The weights then no longer matched the probabilities predict() gives. With n_splits chosen out of bag (n_splits = NULL) and the forest pruned (prune = TRUE), the pruned model’s test log-loss is now about that of logit, often with far fewer splits chosen and a faster fit. Fitted models change for loss = "exponential" with more than two classes only; binary fits are unchanged.

  • purify() with mode = 2 no longer drops training rows that lie on a leaf’s lower bound. Purified components and the intercept now equal those of mode = 1.

  • predict_components() returns a remainder whenever m leaves out components of the forest, also when predictors leaves out some of the fit’s predictors at the fit’s max_interaction. Previously the intercept and m then did not sum to the prediction.

  • predict_components() takes the components’ predictors from the forest’s own columns, in their order. A formula with terms such as log(x1), I(x1^2) or . - x3 no longer makes it fail, and with factor predictors the components come in the order of the fit’s columns, which has the factors last.

  • predict_components() on a new_data with zero rows returns zero rows with the right columns, instead of failing with “Feature vector is empty.”.

  • print() counts the forest’s own predictor columns: with formula terms such as log(x1) or . - x3 it showed the number of raw columns the formula reads.

  • purify() on a forest purified with maxp_interaction = k purifies it again when asked for more orders (all orders by default). Previously it returned the forest unchanged, so the orders above k stayed zero in predict_components(). purify() also checks its arguments when the forest is already purified. A capped forest restored by rpf_unmarshal() without its training data cannot be purified again; asking for more orders is an error that says so.

Documentation

  • ?purify states how the components are identified (the marginal identification over the training rows, Hiabu, Meyer and Wright, 2023), and that the intercept is the mean prediction on the training rows.
  • ?rpf says that deterministic = TRUE also ignores split_decay_rate, how split_structure = "leaves" draws its thresholds, and that a seed reproduces a fit on the same platform only. splits counts rounds: near saturation a round can make no split. Ties between equally good candidates may go to different candidates under the exact and the fast draw, so their fits differ in distribution near saturation, though not in accuracy.
  • ?print.rpf_forest’s example prints a forest (export_forest = TRUE), and ?plot.rpf cites the RPF paper as 2020.

Performance

  • Classification with loss = "logit" fits much faster, with bitwise the same fits. For every candidate split, the logit loss copied the weights of all observations twice, although it reads only those of the leaf being split, so a candidate cost time in proportion to the sample size instead of the leaf size.
  • Fitting regression forests with split_structure = "leaf" (the default) is faster on larger data. Fitted models are bitwise unchanged.
  • predict() is faster for forests that are not purified, with bitwise the same predictions. From 512 rows on, each tree of more than 64 leaves gets an index of its leaves (a k-d tree, built per call), so a row is tested only against the leaves that may hold it instead of against every leaf.
  • Fitting regression forests with split_structure = "tree_then_leaf" is much faster and needs less memory. Fitted models are bitwise unchanged.
  • purify() keeps the purified components as weighted rectangles instead of dense grids over all split points (with mode = 2, the default, which predict_components() and rpf(purify = TRUE) use). Purification at max_interaction = 3 and above needs much less memory and no longer runs out of it on larger data. The components equal those of mode = 1 up to rounding, and rpf_marshal() stores the rectangles.
  • predict_components() evaluates all components in one pass over the rows of new_data, and skips those the forest does not hold, instead of one pass per component, which is faster.
  • Classification uses the split search of regression: one implementation of the five split structures, which differ between the two only in how a candidate split is scored. So classification gets the faster "tree_then_leaf" and "leaf" and the smaller finished forests of regression, with bitwise the same fits.
  • prune_components(), and so rpf(prune = TRUE) and rpf(tune = ), no longer build the purified store of all components. Each tree family is purified in turn, its components are evaluated at the training rows (and out of bag) and then freed, and the pruned model stores the pieces of its kept components only, from which predict() and predict_components() evaluate them. purify() keeps every piece of every component, which grows steeply with the order, so the whole call rpf(n_splits = NULL, prune = TRUE) needs much less memory at high orders, where it could run out of memory while purifying, and less at order 3, in the same time. The pruned models are the same up to rounding: the same choices, kept components and display. The forest in the result is left unpurified (call purify() for all its components), and an earlier purification of it is no longer redone.
  • A fitted forest takes less memory: the split search’s per-leaf caches are kept apart from the leaves and freed when a tree family is finished, so a leaf takes 80 instead of 232 bytes; finished classification forests now also drop their training rows and caches. Fitted models are bitwise unchanged.
  • Classification with loss = "logit" fits faster again, with bitwise the same fits. The terms of the loss under the current weights do not depend on the candidate split, so each observation’s terms are now computed once and refreshed only when its weights change, and the terms of classes the observation is not in (which are zero) are skipped: a candidate takes one exponential per logit column and one logarithm per observation of the leaf, instead of two exponentials and two logarithms per column plus two logarithms.
  • Growing with split_structure = "leaf" (the default) is much faster, with bitwise the same fits. A leaf’s rows are put in order by each row’s integer rank in the predictor (ranked once per tree family) with a radix sort, instead of a comparison sort of the values, and the leaf keeps that order with the first position of each distinct value, so a candidate split no longer passes over the leaf’s values; the thresholds are drawn without allocating memory. Classification gains less.
  • Pruning (prune_components(), and so the default call) is faster on larger data, with bitwise the same models. The numbers of training rows in the leaves’ boxes, counted in the pass over the tree families, are kept for the later passes (the display’s coarsening, its out-of-bag sums, the store of the kept components) instead of being counted again, for trees of up to 4 predictors; and the index of the components’ rectangles finds its cuts without sorting.
  • Choosing the number of splits out of bag (n_splits = NULL, the default) needs much less memory while growing, in the same time and with the same fits. Each tree family’s out-of-bag predictions are added to the checkpoints’ sums as the family delivers them, instead of being kept until the stop is decided; the pool of split candidates keeps no record of its entries; and options(randomPlantedForest.adaptive_pause_gb), the memory of the families waiting for the stop, defaults to 0.25 GB instead of 1 GB.
  • rpf_marshal() of a large forest is several times as fast: the forest’s lists of trees and leaves are allocated at their final lengths instead of grown by one element at a time, which copied each list for every element. The blob is the same.

randomPlantedForest 0.5.0

Breaking changes

  • rpf() now defaults to max_interaction = 2, main effects and pairwise interactions, instead of 1, an additive model (#66). Values above the number of predictors are capped silently instead of with a message.
  • rpf() now defaults to loss = "exponential" for classification instead of "L2", so classification fits give proper probability estimates by default; regression still uses "L2" (#66).
  • rpf() arguments are reordered by purpose (forest size, split search, loss, other). Pass arguments after the data arguments by name (#66).
  • rpf(), predict() and purify() error on unknown arguments, such as misspelled ones, instead of silently ignoring them (#66).
  • purify() is a regular function instead of an S3 generic (#66).
  • preprocess_predictors_predict() is no longer exported; it is an internal step of predict() (#66).
  • The package now requires R >= 4.1.0 (#66).
  • For a given seed, classification models differ from 0.4.0 due to the fixes and speedup below, but regression models are unchanged (#57, #66).
  • For direct users of the C++ object ($fit): set_data() no longer fits, call fit() afterwards, and an unknown classification loss is an error instead of a silent fallback to L2 (@jyliuu, #57).
  • rpf() no longer has a cv argument, which never had an effect: the C++ cross-validation was a no-op (#66).

Bug fixes

  • predict() and predict_components() error on missing values in new_data, naming the affected columns. Previously such rows silently received arbitrary predictions, as rpf() has no handling for missing values. rpf() likewise reports missing values in the training data by column (#66).
  • Classification fits with a fixed seed could differ between runs. When a split replaced a leaf, its new split candidates could be lost or attached to the wrong leaf, depending on memory layout (#66).
  • predict(type = "class") breaks probability ties by level order instead of at random, so class predictions are deterministic and no longer advance the random number generator (#66).
  • purify() returns its input invisibly, as documented (#66).
  • Logical predictors in the formula interface are used as a single 0/1 column, as in the x/y interface. Previously they were expanded into two redundant indicator columns, which also counted against max_interaction (#66).

Performance

  • Prediction is much faster: leaves are scanned from flat, cache-friendly arrays (~15x single-threaded), and rows are split across threads (#65). predict() gains nthreads, defaulting to the nthreads used for fitting.
  • predict_components() is much faster: purified forests look up only the trees of the requested component, and each distinct input row is predicted once, which pays off for low-cardinality features (#59, #65).
  • Classification fits are slightly faster, as redundant work during model construction was removed (#57).

Other improvements

  • New “Getting started” vignette covering regression, classification, component decomposition, recipes, and saving models (#66).
  • The print() method is overhauled and gains a format() counterpart: it reports the forest size, interaction degree, purification state, split search settings and number of threads (#66).
  • deterministic = TRUE with ntrees > 1 warns, as all tree families are then identical (#66).
  • Rewritten documentation for rpf(), purify() and predict_components(), including guidance on choosing parameters and on how purification interacts with predict_components() (#66).

Internals

  • The C++ core no longer depends on Rcpp: it uses standard C++ types and exceptions, and an Rcpp layer (src/rcpp_interface.*) converts at the boundary. This is groundwork for bindings in other languages such as Python (@jyliuu, #57).
  • cli and rlang are now imported, mvtnorm is only needed to build the pkgdown site (#66).

randomPlantedForest 0.4.0

It is now possible to serialize and de-serialize an rpf object via marshalling, meaning a fitted model can be saved to disk or dispatched to a worker process for parallelization or encapsulation, as is done in mlr3. This also re-opens the door for the mlr3extralearners wrapper, which was removed due to the lack of serialization support.

  • New rpf_marshal() / rpf_unmarshal() serialize a fitted forest to a plain R list and back, making saveRDS()-based storage of rpf models possible (#52). Purified forests restore their purified state directly; training data is only embedded with include_data = TRUE (required to purify() after restoring). Blobs record the blob format version and the package version they were created with; restoring under an older package than the one that saved the model warns. Malformed or corrupt blobs error instead of reading out of bounds.
  • New rpf_is_valid() checks whether an rpf object’s internal model is usable, predict(), purify() and predict_components() now give an actionable error for rpf objects restored via readRDS() without marshaling.
  • New bundle::bundle() method for rpf models wrapping the marshaling API.

Behavior changes

  • The default for delta changed from 0 to 0.001. With delta = 0, splits producing single-class nodes have infinite logit loss and are always rejected, which also degraded binary logit fits.

Fixes and improvements

  • Fixed multiclass classification with loss = "logit", which effectively never split and predicted near-uniform class probabilities (#40). The C++ logit loss is a reference-class multinomial formulation expecting K-1 indicator columns, but the R wrapper passed a full K-column one-hot matrix, pinning the implicit reference-class probability to zero. Multiclass logit outcomes are now encoded with the first factor level as reference class:
    • predict(type = "prob") reconstructs all K class probabilities from the K-1 logits; rows sum to 1 exactly.
    • predict(type = "numeric"/"link") now returns K-1 columns named after the non-reference levels (previously K columns).
    • predict_components() on multiclass logit fits returns per-class components for the K-1 non-reference levels; target_levels reflects this.

randomPlantedForest 0.3.0

Major changes (#61)

  • New rpf() arguments controlling split-candidate sampling:
    • split_structure = "leaves": Defines what a split candidate is and how candidates are drawn. One of "leaves" (default), "hist", "cur_trees_1", "cur_trees_2", or "res_trees"; see ?rpf for details.
    • max_candidates = 50: Maximum number of split candidates sampled per iteration.
    • split_decay_rate = 0.1: Exponential aging of repeatedly drawn but unchosen split candidates. split_decay_rate = 0 corresponds to no aging and uniform sampling.
    • delete_leaves = TRUE: Whether a parent leaf is deleted when splitting along an existing dimension.
  • Fitting results change: The new candidate-sampling defaults and a reworked internal RNG mean that fits are not reproducible against previous versions, even with the same seed. Install an older commit if exact reproduction of previous results is required.
  • Seeded fits are now reproducible regardless of nthreads: per-tree seeds are drawn from R’s RNG, so set.seed() gives identical forests for serial and multithreaded fits.
  • Substantial speedups in fitting (cached per-leaf orderings, prefix sums) and reduced memory use (training-only buffers are released after each tree family is built).
  • purify() gains arguments:
    • mode = 2: Purification algorithm; 2 is a new fast exact method, 1 is the legacy grid-based path.
    • nthreads = NULL: Purification is now multithreaded, defaulting to the fit’s nthreads setting.
    • maxp_interaction = NULL: Optionally only compute purified components up to this interaction order.
  • New rpf() argument export_forest = FALSE: The flattened forest is no longer stored in the fitted object by default, so rpf_object$forest is NULL unless export_forest = TRUE. This reduces object size; predict(), purify(), and predict_components() are unaffected.
  • preprocess_predictors_predict() is now exported.
  • Fixed a memory bug in the legacy purification path where the grid was sized one element too large, causing out-of-bounds reads (crashes on Windows, silently wrong purification results elsewhere).
  • Fixed a crash on Windows when fitting with nthreads > 1, caused by a thread_local buffer with a non-trivial destructor being destroyed at thread exit.

Other changes

  • Internals in src/ have been refactored into modular sub-files (#53)
  • rpf() now errors if a regression target is combined with a loss other than "L2".
  • Allow features of type logical, which are now converted via as.integer.
  • The parallel = TRUE|FALSE argument in rpf() has been substituted by an nthreads = 1L argument, allowing for more flexible parallelization. The previous behavior only allowed for either no parallelization or using n-1 of n available cores. The new implementation should be reasonably robust and the default behavior remains serial execution.
  • Remove SystemRequirements field from DESCRIPTION: Now the default C++ version is C++17 and with a minor change to internal use of random numbers, randomPlantedForest is now compatible with C++11 through C++23.
  • Add remainder term to predict_components output for case where max_interaction supplied is smaller than max_interaction in rpf fit. In that case, the m values don’t sum up to the global predictions, so we add a remainder to allow reconstruction of that property.

randomPlantedForest 0.2.1

  • Add glex class to output of predict_components(), for extended functionality available with glex.
  • Add target_levels vector to output of predict_components() to aid multiclass handling. Keeping track of levels is somewhat awkward since column names of $m need to be identifiable regarding the target level.

randomPlantedForest 0.2.0

  • Added a NEWS.md file to track changes to the package.
